articles.headline: Who are the violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank?
keyFacts: Human rights organizations have documented record levels of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank over the past three years.
Journalist Feliz Solomon reported that a group of young settlers known as the Hilltop Youth violently blocked a Palestinian family from returning to their home in Jalud.
While military officials acknowledge the violence is a major problem, human rights organizations and reports note that settlers often act with near-total impunity.
body: A destroyed car sits outside a burnt home in the West Bank village of Jalud on September 29, 2026. | Erik Marmor/Getty Images
In the weeks and months following Hamas’s brutal October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and Israel’s devastating campaign in Gaza that followed, the world’s attention turned away from the West Bank.
Over the past three years, however, the situation in the Israel-occupied territory has worsened as Israeli settlers have carried out more violent attacks on Palestinians .

The attacks can range from acts of daily harassment and trespassing to a major mob assault in the West Bank village of Jalud that overwhelmed Israeli security forces and blocked a displaced Palestinian family from returning home. Last week, Israeli settlers shot and killed a Palestinian man.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has largely dismissed violent West Bank settlers as an issue, blaming the Jalud attack on a “handful of rioters” and referring to settlers as “juvenile delinquents” in a speech to the UN last month , in which he argued that the world should focus on violence committed by Palestinians instead.

But even as he downplays the problem, human rights organizations have documented a record level of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. The International Committee of the Red Cross has said that such attacks have made everyday life “untenable” for the more than 3 million Palestinians living in the West Bank.
The Israeli settlements are also clearly illegal, as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp explained in September — but that hasn’t stopped them from expanding.

Ahead of Israel’s elections later this month, settlers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing with the explicit backing of some Israeli cabinet ministers , led by young militant Jewish settlers that are part of a loose network known as the Hilltop Youth .

The Wall Street Journal’s Feliz Solomon reported on the Jalud attack and has written about the role of Hilltop Youth in worsening settler violence. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the reality on the ground in the West Bank, the settler groups behind it, and how Israeli officials are responding.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .
Tell me about the last three years in the West Bank. What’s been happening?
The October 7 attack really hardened a lot of people’s views in Israel, and that’s played out in the West Bank in a number of ways.
One is that the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, which has some powerful members who are settlers themselves, became much more overtly supportive of expanding the Jewish settlements.

The second thing that changed was basically a total breakdown of trust, both between Jews and Arabs, and also between Jews and the state, because a lot of people felt that they were really on their own in terms of security.

All of this created a really combustible environment. There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.
What does that total impunity look like? We often hear the term “settler violence.” What does that mean?

There’s really a whole spectrum of violent actions. It’s mostly by younger male settlers. There are some acts of daily harassment, like trespassing on Palestinian property, vandalism, stalking people, blocking roads, and preventing access to resources like water wells. And then on the other end of the spectrum, there are also acts of extreme violence.

There have been some very serious physical assaults. Settlers throwing rocks with slingshots. Last year, there was a viral video of an elderly woman who was beaten with a stick. She was hospitalized for days. And lately, we’ve been seeing more mob violence where a large group of settlers will raid a Palestinian village. They’ve set mosques and other property on fire.

Just to be clear, there’s violence by Palestinians too, but we’re really seeing an alarming surge of violence by settlers that’s often unpunished, and increasingly it’s happening when settlers go into Palestinian areas where they’re not supposed to be.
You reported on an attack that happened last week in the West Bank near the Palestinian village of Jalud. Tell me what happened.

Over the summer, some young settlers who are associated with a group called the Hilltop Youth set up an encampment around three houses on the outskirts of the Palestinian village, Jalud, and essentially besieged the houses. They blocked their access to essential goods and harassed the residents until, in late July, they felt so unsafe that they fled.

Two of those houses belonged to the Tubasi family. In early September, Israel’s high court ordered the state to ensure their safe return, and in late September, they tried to go back. We spoke with Wael, who’s one member of the family, and also with their lawyer about what happened when they tried to go back.

A few dozen [Israeli] security forces were deployed to escort them home in the middle of the night, and when they got there, they found that the house was totally ransacked. They showed us before and after pictures, and the windows were smashed, the doors were broken, electrical wires were cut, and there was just debris all over the place.

When they came inside for the first time in about two months, they were walking through the property looking at the damage with flashlights, and they’d only been there for a few minutes when suddenly they were surrounded by a mob of settlers. They said at first that there were about 50 settlers around the house, and the military later said that there were more than a hundred people that took part in what they called a riot.

The authorities told the family to take cover deeper inside the house, and they hid inside a stairwell as the soldiers tried to force these settlers to retreat, but they were shouting and throwing rocks at the house, and then, according to Wael, they even started climbing in through the windows. At that point, the authorities told the family to go upstairs, all the way up to the roof and to hide in a corner of the rooftop.
Wael explained what he saw up there. He was looking down and he saw the soldiers battling it out with this large group of settlers and this thick cloud of tear gas and loud bangs from stun grenades.
“There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.”

Eventually, the security forces realized that they weren’t getting the situation under control. They had to get this family out of there. They took them back downstairs and outside and put them in a military vehicle, but then the settlers surrounded the vehicle and they were rocking the car. They slashed the tires so that [the family] couldn’t leave. Then the soldiers had to move them into an armored military vehicle and eventually they got them out.

A short while later, not long after they had escaped, they started receiving video messages from some of their neighbors that showed what happened after they left, which was that their car and their house had been set on fire.

All right, so the Israeli authorities in the form of soldiers were trying to help this Palestinian family legally return and settlers violently blocked them. This is settlers versus the authorities. What do we know about who these settlers are and what is motivating them?
This was a very large group. We know of three people who were detained in this incident. All of them were teenagers. The youngest one I believe was 15 years old.

A lot of the harassment in this area comes out of a nearby settlement called Esh Kodesh and smaller, more informal settlements around it that are called outposts. And these outposts are usually pretty crude encampments. They often start with just tents or a camper van or a trailer with no electricity and no water. And the people who choose to live in these places tend to be very young, very extreme ideological settlers.
You mentioned something called the Hilltop Youth. Who are they?

The Hilltop Youth is a loose network of settlers that live outside the mainstream, and they often have much more extremist views than the mainstream settler movement. It’s an offshoot of religious Zionism, which is one of the main ideologies of the settler movement, and it sort of fuses the ideas of Orthodox Judaism with ultranationalism.

The Hilltop Youth take these ideas to the extreme, and I’ve spoken with a bunch of them myself. They believe that they’re on a divine mission to reclaim the Holy Land for Jews, and they’ll cite parts of the Torah and other religious texts that they interpret as empowering them to take the land back and even to use violence. They see it as a preventive type of self-defense, and they see themselves as protecting all other Jews.
These are young people, some of them teenagers. Where are they coming from? Why are their parents not grounding them? How has this been allowed to unfold the way it has?

It’s a good question, and I should say also that not all Hilltop Youth are violent, but a lot of the violence that’s committed by Jews in the West Bank does come from this group, and they come from all over the place. Some of them grew up in the settlements, and then as teenagers, they kind of wandered and they struck out on their own. And then there are others who come from all over Israel.

A lot of the Hilltop Youth, we’re finding, are kind of troubled kids. Sometimes they’re dropouts from strict religious schools, sometimes they have behavioral issues or ADHD, and they just didn’t really fit in. We heard from some kids who said that they found out about the outposts by word of mouth, like someone at their school had invited them to come for the weekend and they’d come and they’d stay a few days and eventually they’d start spending more and more time there until at some point they’re just living there.

There are a number of NGOs that recruit young kids to come work as farm hands on agricultural outposts in the West Bank, and some of those are in these areas that are more prone to radicalization. These organizations present themselves as very innocent in that they’re identifying kids that need help and are bringing them to a place where they will learn some discipline and they will have a purpose and they’ll have something to do. But that often puts them into a more extreme environment.

In the case of the family you profiled in Jalud, it’s clear that the Israeli authorities, in the form of soldiers, attempted to help the family get back to their home. How does this typically play out, though? How do Israeli soldiers typically respond when settlers attack Palestinians?
There have been a number of high-profile examples of video footage circulating that appears to show Israeli soldiers either standing idly by or even, some would argue, siding with the settlers.

In one recent example, there was a video that showed some soldiers praying alongside settlers who had besieged the home of a Palestinian American man, and that was actually not very far from where the Tubasi house is. The military said that it was looking into it to determine whether disciplinary action needed to be taken.

In general, military officials acknowledge that this violence by settlers is a big problem, and the security establishment definitely does not support what’s happening here. They see it as getting in the way of counter-terrorism efforts and overall efforts to bring stability to this very volatile area.

I’ve heard this directly from military officers, but on the ground there does seem to be a breakdown of discipline in some cases and a lack of clear instruction in other cases. Some soldiers simply don’t know how to deal with threats from other Israelis, especially really young ones, as you pointed out. It’s just not what they’re trained to do.
Do you think the government could put a stop to these attacks by settlers if it wanted to, or has the government lost control?

This problem has gotten so big that it’s going to be very difficult to solve without significant backlash, but I have spoken with a number of former Israeli security officials who say yes, much more could be done — starting with a more frank acknowledgement of what’s happening, clearer law enforcement procedures, and more disciplinary actions.

articles.headline: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
keyFacts: Sara Tashakorinia founded the startup LumenUs to help grieving families automate the administrative paperwork required after a death.
LumenUs uses AI to organize tasks by urgency and help users navigate legal, financial, and insurance processes during grief.
The startup will launch in early access in October and is participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 showcase.
body: When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work.

“The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch.

After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.
The result is LumenUs, the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden.

“I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said.

While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation.

“We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said.

From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available.
“We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said.

Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product.

LumenUs, a participant in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 — the annual showcase of promising early-stage startups at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco — will launch in early access in October.

articles.headline: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
keyFacts: Global leaders are asking for information after a lab technician died in Russia amid unverified rumors of plague exposure.
The World Health Organization invoked international regulations requiring countries to share health information that could have international implications.
Russia did not initially notify the World Health Organization about the death, and experts note the international law lacks an enforcement mechanism.
body: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.

The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.
Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.
But there are still far more questions than answers.

That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.
On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.
Rooted in the 19th century

This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.

"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."

Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.
A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.

Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)
One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.
Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.
Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.
The situation in Russia
Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.
However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.
"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."

It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.

WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.

Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.

That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin, who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.
"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.
"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."

He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

articles.headline: Edwards joins Argentina as defence coach
keyFacts: Shaun Edwards has joined Argentina's coaching staff as defence coach on a deal running until the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup.
Edwards will finish his consultancy role with England's women's team before starting work with Argentina at the end of October alongside Mario Ledesma.
Argentina are scheduled to play Nations Championship matches against Ireland, Italy and France in November.
body: - Published
Defence coach Shaun Edwards has joined Argentina's coaching staff on a deal that runs until the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia.

The announcement ends any speculation that Edwards could be handed a role in Steve Borthwick's England set-up, with the 59-year-old set to fulfil his consultancy role with England's women's team before joining Felipe Contepomi's staff.
"I'm delighted to join Felipe Contepomi, his coaching staff and the Argentina rugby team at the end of this month until the World Cup next year in Australia," said Edwards.
"I've always admired the ability and quality of Argentine players and I hope to bring some of my international experience to the team during the next year," added the former Wigan rugby league great.
Englishman Edwards, who is one of the most decorated coaches in rugby union, left his position as France men's defence coach earlier this year after helping them win three Six Nations titles.
Edwards and former Argentina head coach and hooker Mario Ledesma, who has been appointed to take charge of the forwards, will start work with the Pumas at the end of October.
Argentina are then set to face Ireland, Italy and France in November in Nations Championship matches.
Three-time semi-finalists Argentina have been drawn in a pool with Fiji, Spain and Canada at the World Cup which takes place between 1 October and 13 November in 2027.

Edwards, who also spent a successful 12 years with Wales and won four English titles and two Champions Cups while on Wasps' staff, said in March that he was interested in coaching in the Rugby Championship, the southern hemisphere tournament contested by South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina.
He turned down a chance to coach his country in 2006, believing that the busier fixture list at Wasps would suit him better as he grieved the death of his brother.
Two years later, he opted to take on a defence role with Wales, rather than lead England's second-string side, then known as the Saxons., external
In 2021, he met with Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney but, without a firm offer forthcoming, signed a contract extension to stay with France.

articles.headline: Wolff tells critics to ‘watch Teletubbies or Mickey Mouse not F1’ as he defends Mercedes’ strategy
keyFacts: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff condemned online accusations of bias regarding his management of drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.
Russell starts Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid following engine penalties from a failure in Malaysia.
Mercedes split their car upgrade options for the weekend to help diagnose development issues with their newer package.
body: Toto Wolff has condemned accusations of bias in how he has managed his drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, with the Mercedes team principal describing those positing such theories as better off watching “Teletubbies or Mickey Mouse” rather than Formula One.

With Antonelli leading Russell by 84 points in the world championship as they go into this weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix, the Italian’s first title is within his reach. The 20-year-old has driven superbly in only his second season in F1 but Russell has struggled with poor fortune and reliability issues that have stymied his championship challenge.

At the last round, in Malaysia, an engine failure cost Russell a potential podium spot and led to a host of accusations online of bias towards Antonelli. Speaking in Singapore, Wolff’s exasperation was clear.

“They’re brainless, whoever thinks that, it’s completely nonsensical,” he said. “I don’t know what’s going on. Do they think I have a button that says: ‘George, engine failure now’? Or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a constructors’ championship when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material?

“There’s a lot of polarisation and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I’m Satan, I’ve heard. So, overall funny. But really, zero understanding and respect for people who come up with these things. Rather than watching Formula One, they should do Teletubbies or some Mickey Mouse.”

Russell goes into Sunday’s night race on the Marina Bay circuit clinging on in the title fight. Not only did the engine failure cost him in Malaysia but it meant he has had to take a new engine for this race and with the attendant penalties will have to start from the back of the grid on a track where overtaking is enormously tricky.

Mercedes have further complications in Singapore. The upgrades they brought to Malaysia did not prove effective and have left the team somewhat perplexed as to why they had not delivered. They opted, with Russell’s approval, to split their options this weekend with the British driver reverting to the spec with which he had won in Baku and Antonelli running the new version in order to provide an insight into where the developments were wanting.

In qualifying for Saturday’s sprint race, Russell was clearly enjoying his pre-upgrade ride more than his teammate. He took second on the grid with Antonelli only in seventh, while Max Verstappen took an excellent pole to back up his win at Sepang. Antonelli certainly felt he was somewhat under the cosh in Singapore with a car far removed from what he is used to. “There is still a lot to understand about this package, the car is very difficult, very unpredictable,” he said. “I was coming in with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult. It’s going to be a difficult weekend, it’s going to be very tricky. I don’t see where we can find seven-tenths.”

Mercedes are clear they will continue to allow their drivers to race one another. Wolff, who managed three seasons of increasingly intense and rancorous rivalry between Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg between 2014 and 2016, has always been insistent that he has practised even-handed management since he joined F1. He cited a conversation he had with Alain Prost about his bitter rivalry with Ayrton Senna while at McLaren in the 1980s.

“I remember being a complete rookie and running into Alain Prost on the grid of a race and I said: ‘Why did it go so wrong between you and Senna?’ He said: ‘Because we never knew what the team was about. You felt that you were the flavour of the month one time and then two months later you thought the politics were going against you. There were different situations where you had the feeling that you’re really not wanted.’

“So, I took it as my challenge to keep it always balanced and it was not easy with Lewis and Nico back in the day. That’s why people can think what they want but the integrity in that respect is something that’s important for me, and the drivers know it.”

Russell has admitted Antonelli has done a better job overall this season, while also noting that he would have expected to still be in the fight were it not for some of the problems he has suffered. He looked quick on the Marina Bay circuit on Friday but still has a huge task to come through the field on Sunday.

Antonelli’s advantage is such that if he is 101 points ahead after this meeting, he could become F1’s youngest world champion at the next round in Austin. A title, as Wolff would doubtless attest, that will have been won purely on merit.

articles.headline: Microsoft 365 subscribers set to lose up to 4TB of OneDrive storage
keyFacts: Microsoft announced changes to OneDrive shared storage allotments that reduce total capacity for Family, Premium, and Pro tiers.
Fully shared Family and Premium subscriptions will lose up to 4TB of combined storage, while Pro subscriptions will lose up to 1TB.
New subscribers see the new storage quotas immediately, while existing subscribers will be affected when their plans renew on or after May 2, 2027.
body: Microsoft 365 subscribers on Family, Premium, or Pro tiers who make full use of their OneDrive storage allotments consider this a warning: It’s fixin’ to shrink. Redmond published a support page this week detailing changes to Microsoft 365 shared storage allotments, and while the company is painting them as offering greater flexibility for users, they also represent a massive reduction in capacity. The former storage allotment schema offered 1TB per user on all three of those tiers, with a cap of six users, for a total of 6TB. The new storage quotas will be shared among all users on those accounts, still with a six-user cap. Family or Premium plans now get 2TB of storage space to share among up to six users. Pro tier users will have to share 5TB. In effect, that means fully shared Family and Premium subscriptions will lose up to 4 TB of combined storage capacity, while Pro subscriptions will lose up to 1 TB. Some existing customers may qualify for temporary bonus storage. On the plus side, there's no longer a fixed 1 TB cap per person, provided the shared pool has room. “The goal is to provide a more flexible experience,” Microsoft offers as its justification for the move. “Shared storage helps ensure that one person doesn't run out of space while other members have unused storage available.” That might be great for heavy users on an account, who can now go over a 1TB cap, but if, say, four people on a family plan are all using 500GB and someone wants to upload something else, that’s too bad. You can always buy more OneDrive space, of course. Microsoft appears to understand that users might see this as a reduction in storage, posing an FAQ question: "Is this change a reduction in storage?" The answer again highlights "flexibility," and helpfully notes, "For example, if the subscription owner doesn't share the plan, they can use the full shared storage allotment." (Individual plans already exist but top out at 1TB.) Microsoft also appears to understand that the move might cause a backlash, and has included subscription cancellation steps right on the support page for the change. New Family, Premium, and Pro tier subscribers as of Thursday will see this new storage allotment schema. Existing subscribers will be hit with the change when their plans renew on or after May 2, 2027. Microsoft said it will remind users of the change as their renewal date approaches. Customers are not thrilled about this move. A thread on Reddit discussing the change has nothing positive to say about it, with commenters noting that they’re likely to cancel their subscriptions rather than let them renew and face a storage reduction and a need to clean up files. Much of the Microsoft365 subreddit, as of writing, is filled with posts complaining about the move, with one of the top posts reminding people to turn off their automatic renewal to avoid getting hit with the storage slash. The Windows maker has a semi-regular habit of slashing cloud storage allotments for its 365 customers. Office 365 used to come with unlimited cloud storage, but that offer ended after some users actually took unlimited to mean unlimited. Storage tiers have been further reduced over the years, most recently in 2024 when McGill University drastically slashed students' OneDrive allowances to 20 GB following Microsoft's changes to education storage allocations. In other words, don’t get too comfortable with 2TB of shared storage for six people – that deal, too, may be altered further. ®

articles.headline: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
keyFacts: Nikon disqualified a winning microscopic video by Dr Ning Xu after scientists raised concerns that it was fake.
Nikon stated that the winning entry broke competition rules regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence.
Nikon announced it will review the rules and procedures of the annual contest following the controversy.
body: - Published
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
The BBC has approached him for comment.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

articles.headline: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay
keyFacts: South African legal pioneer Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for defending international law.
Pillay's career includes defending Nelson Mandela against apartheid and leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Despite turning 85 last month, Pillay stated that she has no intention of stopping her work.
body: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world where increasingly “might overtakes right.”

Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay

Using the award to make a wider point about geopolitics, Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”

Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.

That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s longstanding ambitions to win the Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.
“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said, adding that despite turning 85 last month she had no intention of doing so.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said to cheers.

“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”
Having just been told the news, she added jokingly, “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was in Germany and among the first people to tell Pillay she had won.

“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC” and she led the U.N. commission, “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”

Pillay was not among the pre-announcement frontrunners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba, who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly deported by Russia.
Trump was among the 287 candidates, according to the leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia, who said they nominated him. But Trump said this week he didn’t think he would win.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
